results.content: To post you must register, providing your **real** first and last names. # Using Net Benefit and Decision Curve Analysis to pre-specify target model performance. You have selected **0** posts. I’ve seen some studies pre-specify sensitivity (Se) and specificity (Sp) targets for calling their predictive models useful. For instance, the CCGA study from GRAIL Inc. specified they wanted 99% specificity and “useful sensitivity” without much formal justification. Feels like a better alternative would be to define targets based on the net benefit itself given an appropriate decision threshold. If we want to stick with things like Se/Sp, we could still use the net benefit to elicitate the desired targets. Suppose you want to develop a cancer diagnostic model that potentially refers people to a biopsy for confirmation of aggressive disease. In the population of interest, the prevalence of this aggressive cancer is 30%; for the model, your team agrees on a decision threshold of 10%. The net benefit of biopsying all patients (the current standard of care) is then:. For a calibrated model, you now have a lower bound for your required performance which *a priori* takes into account the clinical context through the elicitation of the relevant decision threshold. During validation, there must be enough evidence that your model beats the Treat all strategy, i.e., the net benefit of your model has to be higher than 0.22 (assuming not test harm for simplicity). Here, net benefit gain means the model’s net benefit at threshold 10% is greater than 0.222. So, for instance, if your sensitivity turns out to be 80%, the specificity would have to be at least 77% for your net benefit to be higher than 0.222. One could further restrict this “acceptance region” by excluding non-sensical tests (e.g., where Se + Sp < 1). On the other hand, why would we specify performance targets in terms of discrimination instead of net benefit (or other utility functions)? get_nb <- function(.se, .sp, .p, .t) .se*.p - (1-.sp)*(1-.p)*(.t/(1-.t)). mutate(nb = get_nb(se, sp, 0.3, 0.1)). ggplot(aes(se, sp, color = ifelse(nb > 0.222, "Yes", "No"))) +. labs(color = "Net benefit gain?", x = "Sensitivity", y = "Specificity") +. results.content: About POLARIS   Thinking in Systems   CDC Policy Process   Policy Resources and Trainings   Economic Evaluation   Health Topics   View Menu. # Cost-Benefit Analysis. * Compares intervention cost and benefits to determine health outcomes monetary value. ## What is cost-benefit analysis? Cost-benefit analysis is a way to compare the costs and benefits of an intervention, where both are expressed in monetary units. However, CBA places a monetary value on health outcomes so that both costs and benefits are in monetary units (such as dollars). * **Benefits** including those resulting from an intervention, such as medical costs averted, productivity gains, and the monetized value of health improvements. CBA provides the net benefits (benefits minus costs) of an intervention. ## Cost-Benefit Analysis Example. CBA's estimated net benefit offers a sense of the economic value provided to society by an intervention. Decision makers can also use CBA to compare health and non-health interventions because both costs and benefits are expressed in monetary units.

results.title: Pros :) and Cons :( of Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) for Clinical Decision-Making
results.content:
Khullar
1430 subscribers
23 likes
1601 views
31 Dec 2021
Decision Curve Analysis (DCA), is a novel approach (that improves upon traditional predictive machine learning model evaluation approaches like Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, etc. for evaluating the clinical net benefit of using various prediction models) that was developed by Dr. Andrew J. Vickers and Dr. Elena B. Elkins (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17099194/) in November, 2006. That is, DCA is a powerful approach for evaluating the costs of a False Positive (FP:  wrongly predicting a patient has a disease when they actually do not (and are healthy)...patient incurs unnecessary treatment and side effects, cost, stress, etc.) and a False Negative (FN: wrongly predicting that a diseased patient is instead healthy...patient's condition could deteriorate; for example the cancer could progress to advanced stage).  DCA allows us to evaluate models based on how we weigh the costs of FP and FN mistakes, subjectively, using the notion of probability thresholds. For more clarity on probability thresholds, please see Saniya's video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VJOq_ezsOIs&t=15s.

In this video, Saniya focuses on the main Pros (strengths :) ) as well as the main Cons (weaknesses :( ) of Decision Curve Analysis.  Please note that these are important things to be considered.  And often, DCA works well in conjunction with other model evaluation approaches.  So, Saniya humbly believes that while DCA is indeed an invaluable tool, other machine learning evaluation models do hold their own merits and should also be used for a more holistic evaluation. 

Also, please note that this was not mentioned in the video, but Saniya wanted to add that although i mention there is no main method for correcting decision curve analysis for being overfit, there are some different methods for correcting for overfit models (https://bmcmedinformdecismak.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1472-6947-8-53): 
"We therefore recommend repeated 10-fold cross-validation as a method to correct decision curves created using the same data as that used to generate the model.'

Further, to clarify: A net benefit of x means that your model / test / whatever is the equivalent of a strategy that found 100 x for every 100 patients without any patient having a false positive. For instance, if the decision curve is about cancer biopsy, and at a given threshold net benefit for a model was 0.20, you'd say that using the model is the equivalent of doing 20 biopsies per 100 and every single one had cancer, there were no negative biopsies. You can say the same about difference in net benefit. In the biopsy example, if the net benefit between model A and model B was 0.01 at a 10% threshold, you'd say that using model A rather than model B was the equivalent of finding one extra cancer per 100 for the same number of biopsies. You can also convert difference in net benefit to the unit of false positives, rather than true positives but dividing net benefit by pt /(1 – pt). so our difference between model A and model B would be 0.09 and you could say "using model A rather than model B is the equivalent of doing 9 fewer biopsies per 100 but finding the same number of cancers".

Saniya does have other introductory videos on DCA and examples of the application of DCA so please do see Saniya's playlist on Decision Curve Analysis (DCA): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL_3UUp3wcnVYYQUQ5wXgNjkl1LI1mocA3

In this video, Saniya is mostly focused on how to interpret the net benefit on the treated in clinical terms and goes over the example provided in the paper by Vickers et. al.  

Please subscribe to Saniya's YouTube channel for more updates :).  Please reach out with any and all questions and concerns ye may have.  Also, to learn more about Decision Curve Analysis, please do check out this link: www.dec...
